newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican coffee growers seek to derail import plans.
newsitem.headline: Mexican coffee growers seek to derail import plans.

text.p: Mexican coffee roasters' plans to import 150,000 60-kg bags of robustas have come up against a wall of opposition from national growers that could derail the imports, growers and traders said Wednesday.
Growers claim that roasters are only trying to avoid paying current high bean prices in their drive to import cheaper robustas for soluble production.

"It is all a question of price. Roasters do not want to pay the current high prices for mild arabicas so they are pushing to import cheaper robustas," said one Mexican trader who declined to be named.
Traders said the government had been bending toward roaster sentiment because it did not want roasters to pass on high prices to customers, impacting inflation and the wider economy.

Ruben Castillo Fragaso, executive president of the Mexican Coffee Council, told Reuters last week that the council and Trade and Agriculture Ministries have approved tariff-free imports of 150,000 bags of robustas between July and September this year - prior to the 1997-1998 crop starting in October.
Castillo Fragaso, the hands-on head of the umbrella group for the entire sector, said roasters had now to apply for individual import permits.
But that position seems to be wavering under pressure from growers.
Agriculture Minister Francisco Labastida Ochoa told the daily El Financiero that a decision still had yet to be taken on imports.
Labastida Ochoa said he had instructed Castillo Fragaso to meet with disgruntled growers and import-hungry roasters, talk through the problem, and then take a decision.
"It is a tricky political situation but there are signs that the government has started to listen to the growers," one trader said, pointing to the less-than-watertight import approval.
A spokesman for the National Coordinating Council of Coffee Organisations (CNOC), the most voluminous coffee growers group in Mexico, said producers were united in their stance against imports.
CNOC adviser Fernando Solis said that eight growers groups had formally written to the government to oppose the import plan.

Solis said Mexican growers calculated there were still around 400,000 bags of Mexican beans left in the country from the 1996-1997 crop and argued that even though there was not much coffee still in Mexico from the 1996-1997 crop, the imports were not needed.

One trader said he thought that growers' estimate on the high side and also a little misleading. The trader, who asked to remain nameless, reckoned around 100,000 bags were still uncommitted in Mexico. "There is a big difference between beans in the country and beans that have no buyer," he added.
Traders said national roasters had effectively stopped buying Mexican beans. One said roasters had recently only been offering prices upto 40 percent lower than international markets.

Carlos Bracamontes, of the National Association of Coffee Growers, told Reforma daily that if robusta imports were to enter Mexico tariff-free, rather than apply a 20 percernt tariff in place, the government would lose revenues of 44 million pesos.
Coffee sources said that roasters had already carved up the 150,000 import quota.
Compania Nestle, the Mexican subsidiary of Swiss-based Nestle, had been given the lion's share with a quota equivalent to 49.5 percent (4.5 million kgs).

Other major quota holders are Sabormex 954,900 kg (10.6 percent), Cafe Internacional de Cordoba 716,640 kgs (8 percent), Cafe El Marino 477,780 kgs (5.3 percent) and Cafe El Pacifico 447,720 kgs (5 percent).
Spokesmen for Nestle in Mexico and the National Coffee Industry Association, Mexico's roaster group, were not immediately available for comment.
